words.definition: Treating everyone in a way that is fair and just to all.
words.example: The mediator proposed an equitable split of the inheritance so neither sibling felt cheated.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'equal' + 'able' — able to keep things equal for everyone.

words.definition: An unfair tendency to favor one person or side over another.
words.example: The referee's obvious partiality toward the home team infuriated the visiting fans.
words.mnemonic: You take only a 'part' of the truth — you take a side.

words.definition: Payment or return of something to make up for loss or damage caused.
words.example: The court ordered the thief to pay restitution to every family he had robbed.
words.mnemonic: RE-STITUTION — you re-institute, put back, whatever you took.

words.definition: Punishment inflicted on someone as deserved payback for a wrong.
words.example: Fearing retribution from his old boss, the whistleblower asked to stay anonymous.
words.mnemonic: RE-TRIBUTION — a 'tribute' paid back in pain for a crime.

words.definition: To bring someone before a court to answer a criminal charge.
words.example: The suspect was arraigned on Monday and entered a plea of not guilty.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a reign' — the law's reign summons you to stand and answer.

words.definition: To carry a dispute through the courts as a lawsuit.
words.example: Rather than settle, the company chose to litigate the patent claim for years.
words.mnemonic: LITI-gate — open the 'gate' to court and fight it out.

words.definition: Meant to make someone suffer a penalty for a wrong.
words.example: The league imposed a punitive fine far larger than the damage warranted.
words.mnemonic: Think 'punitive' → a 'punch' delivered as a penalty.

words.definition: Willing to be gentle and forgiving rather than harsh in punishment.
words.example: The judge was surprisingly lenient, giving the first-time offender only community service.
words.mnemonic: LENIENT sounds like 'lean' — a lean, light penalty that goes easy on you.

words.definition: Mercy or kindness shown by someone with the power to punish.
words.example: The governor granted clemency, sparing the prisoner from execution.
words.mnemonic: Picture a calm, 'clement' (mild) sky — a mild response instead of a storm of punishment.

words.definition: An official act releasing a person from punishment for a crime.
words.example: After new evidence emerged, the president issued a full pardon to the convicted man.
words.mnemonic: PAR-DON — the 'don' (boss) declares you 'par', even again, slate wiped.

words.definition: An official promise to forgive a group for past offenses.
words.example: The new government offered amnesty to rebels who surrendered their weapons.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'amne-' with 'amnesia' — the state chooses to forget your offense.

words.definition: To make an offense appear less serious by offering partial excuses.
words.example: Her youth and genuine fear that night may extenuate what she did.
words.mnemonic: EX-TENU-ate — like 'tenuous' (thin); you thin out the blame.

words.definition: To ease the severity of something without removing its underlying cause.
words.example: The medicine could only palliate his symptoms, never stop the disease itself.
words.mnemonic: A 'pall' (cloak) laid over pain to cover it, not cure it.

words.definition: Extremely severe and cruel, especially regarding rules or penalties.
words.example: The school's draconian phone rule meant confiscation for a single glance at a screen.
words.mnemonic: Named for Draco, the Greek lawmaker whose code punished trivial crimes with death.

words.definition: The practice of giving jobs or favors to one's own relatives.
words.example: Critics cried nepotism when the CEO named his inexperienced nephew as director.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'nepos' (nephew) — hiring your nephew over better candidates.

words.definition: The unfair practice of giving jobs and favors to close friends rather than qualified people.
words.example: After the mayor hired three college buddies as deputies, critics denounced the blatant cronyism at city hall.
words.mnemonic: A CRONY is a longtime pal — cronyism is when your pals quietly get all the perks.

words.definition: Willing to do dishonest things in exchange for money.
words.example: The venal inspector waved the unsafe truck through the moment he spotted the envelope of cash.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like VEND — a venal person is for sale, like a vending machine that dispenses favors for coins.

words.definition: To obtain money or something by using threats or pressure.
words.example: The gang tried to extort the shopkeeper, demanding weekly payments to keep his windows unbroken.
words.mnemonic: ex- + TORT (a wrong, a twist) — you twist someone's arm to squeeze the money out.

words.definition: To harass or oppress someone cruelly, often for their beliefs or identity.
words.example: The regime began to persecute anyone who practiced the banned religion, jailing worshippers without trial.
words.mnemonic: per- (thoroughly) + SECUTE (pursue, as in 'prosecute') — to relentlessly pursue someone in order to harm them.

words.definition: To single someone out for unfair or harmful treatment.
words.example: Older residents were victimized by scammers who emptied their savings through fake phone calls.
words.mnemonic: victim + -ize — literally 'to turn a person into a victim.'

words.definition: A complaint about unfair treatment, or the resentment such treatment causes.
words.example: The workers filed a formal grievance after being denied the overtime pay their contract promised.
words.mnemonic: From GRIEVE — a grievance is a sore point that grieves you until you speak up about it.

words.definition: An unproven claim that someone has done something wrong.
words.example: The newspaper printed the allegation that the senator took bribes, though no evidence was ever shown.
words.mnemonic: Say it as 'a-LEDGE-ation' — a claim so shaky you can't yet stand on the ledge of it.

words.definition: The official decision reached at the end of a trial.
words.example: After three days of deliberation, the jury delivered its verdict: not guilty on all counts.
words.mnemonic: VER (Latin 'verus', truth) + DICT (to say) — a verdict is 'the truth spoken' aloud.

words.definition: A court's decision that a person is not guilty of a crime.
words.example: The defendant wept with relief at her acquittal and walked out of the courtroom a free woman.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-QUIT-al' — the court lets you QUIT the charges and go free.

words.definition: A special court or panel set up to settle certain disputes or cases.
words.example: The war crimes tribunal heard testimony from survivors before sentencing the former general.
words.mnemonic: From the Roman TRIBUNE — the raised platform where officials sat to judge the people.

words.definition: The branch of government responsible for interpreting laws and settling legal disputes.
words.example: An independent judiciary lets courts rule fairly without pressure from politicians.
words.mnemonic: Spot JUDGE hiding inside it — the judiciary is the whole system where judges work.

words.definition: To officially cancel or withdraw a law.
words.example: Lawmakers voted to repeal the outdated curfew, so it no longer applies to anyone.
words.mnemonic: RE- + PEEL — to peel a law back off the books after it was stuck on.

words.definition: To formally do away with a law, treaty, or agreement.
words.example: The new leader threatened to abrogate the peace treaty his predecessor had signed.
words.mnemonic: ab- (away) + rogate (propose, as in 'interrogate') — to officially propose a deal away.

words.definition: To declare officially that something no longer has legal force.
words.example: The couple asked a judge to annul their marriage after learning it was never legally valid.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-NULL' — to reduce something to NULL, to zero, as if it never existed.

words.definition: To make something lose its legal force or effect.
words.example: A single missing signature was enough to nullify the entire contract.
words.mnemonic: NULL + -ify — to make something null, turning it into nothing.

words.definition: To officially cancel the validity of something previously granted.
words.example: After three speeding tickets, the court moved to revoke her driver's license.
words.mnemonic: re- (back) + -voke (to call, as in 'invoke') — you call back what you once gave.

words.definition: To reject a lower decision by exercising greater authority.
words.example: The judge overruled the objection and let the witness answer the question.
words.mnemonic: 'over' + 'rule' — a higher power rules OVER the smaller decision and cancels it.

words.definition: To remove oneself from a matter because of a conflict of interest.
words.example: The judge chose to recuse himself because the defendant was his own cousin.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'excuse' — you politely excuse yourself and step out of the room.

words.definition: Guided by strong moral standards and clear ethical beliefs.
words.example: A principled reporter, she refused the bribe even though no one would ever have known.
words.mnemonic: Someone built on firm inner rules — their conduct always traces back to those rules.

words.definition: A minor breaking of a rule or law.
words.example: Parking on the yellow line is a small infraction, but it still earns a ticket.
words.mnemonic: in-FRACT-ion — a FRACTURE in the rules; something small got broken.

words.definition: Wrongdoing or misconduct, especially by someone holding public office.
words.example: The mayor was charged with malfeasance after quietly diverting city funds into his own account.
words.mnemonic: MAL (bad) + feasance (a doing) — literally 'bad doing' by someone in power.

words.definition: Grave injustice or profound wickedness.
words.example: The prophet railed against the iniquity of a city that let its poor starve in the streets.
words.mnemonic: in-EQUITY — the opposite of equity and fairness; a deep, unjust evil.

words.definition: Moral corruption and a total absence of decency.
words.example: The novel exposes the depravity of men who felt no shame at even the cruelest acts.
words.mnemonic: Think 'deprave' — to strip away all goodness until only rot remains.

words.definition: Extreme baseness or vileness of character.
words.example: He was disbarred for moral turpitude after defrauding his elderly clients for years.
words.mnemonic: TURP sounds like 'turd' — a truly foul, disgusting kind of character.

words.definition: Deserving strong criticism or blame.
words.example: Leaving the injured cyclist alone on the road was reprehensible.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'apprehend' — behavior bad enough to be grabbed and called out.

words.definition: Shockingly evil or utterly monstrous.
words.example: The jury heard details of a crime so heinous that several members began to weep.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'HEY-nus' — 'HEY! that's horrifying!' — a hateful, shocking act.

words.definition: Extremely unpleasant and deserving of hatred.
words.example: Ranking her two best friends was an odious task that left everyone resentful.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'odor' — it stinks so badly that you can't help but hate it.

words.definition: Deserving contempt and utterly low in character.
words.example: Stealing the donations meant for orphans was a despicable thing to do.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'despise' inside it — something you look down on completely.

words.definition: To attack someone with harsh, abusive language.
words.example: The coach began to vituperate the referee, hurling insults until he was ejected.
words.mnemonic: 'viper' + 'utter' — you utter venomous, snake-like words at someone.

words.definition: To protest or argue forcefully against something one opposes.
words.example: She remonstrated with the manager about the unfair firing of her coworker.
words.mnemonic: Like 'demonstrate' against something — you visibly show your objection.

words.definition: To prove that a person is free from blame or guilt for a wrongdoing.
words.example: The new DNA evidence finally exculpated the man who had spent years in prison.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out) + Latin culpa (fault): to take the fault OUT of someone.

words.definition: Freedom from any punishment or harmful consequence for one's actions.
words.example: The dictator's cronies looted the treasury with impunity, certain no court would touch them.
words.mnemonic: im- (not) + 'pun' sounds like PUNish + -ity: the state of 'not being punished.'

words.definition: Patient self-control and tolerance shown when one has been provoked or wronged.
words.example: She handled the screaming customer with remarkable forbearance, never once raising her voice.
words.mnemonic: for-BEAR-ance: picture a huge bear that chooses NOT to attack — holding back.

words.definition: To secretly steal money that an employer or organization trusted you to handle.
words.example: The accountant embezzled thousands by quietly funneling company funds into a private account.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'em-BEZEL': imagine a clerk prying jewels from a ring's bezel at work.

words.definition: To bribe or secretly persuade someone to commit perjury or another unlawful act.
words.example: The lawyer was disbarred for trying to suborn a witness into lying under oath.
words.mnemonic: sub- (secretly, under) + 'orn' ~ ORDER: to secretly order someone to do wrong.

words.definition: Far greater in amount or price than is reasonable or fair.
words.example: They charged an exorbitant fee for a single bottle of water at the airport.
words.mnemonic: ex- + ORBIT: a price so high it has left Earth's orbit and shot into space.

words.definition: Impossible to bribe or morally degrade; firmly and unshakably honest.
words.example: The incorruptible judge returned every gift and ruled strictly on the facts.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + corruptible: simply 'cannot be bought.'

words.definition: A person who behaves wickedly or breaks the law.
words.example: The shopkeeper chased the miscreant who had smashed the window and grabbed the till.
words.mnemonic: mis- (bad) + 'creant' (believe, as in credence): originally a 'bad believer,' now a villain.

words.definition: A morally unprincipled person who feels no shame about bad behavior.
words.example: The old reprobate spent his nights gambling and his mornings sleeping off the wine.
words.mnemonic: re- + 'probate' ~ PROVE: someone who fails the moral test — stamped 'not approved.'

words.definition: The use of clever tricks and deception to cheat or mislead someone.
words.example: The contract was full of legal chicanery designed to trap customers in hidden fees.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'chic canary': a slick little bird singing sweet lies to trick you.

words.definition: Likely to provoke resentment or ill will because it seems unfair.
words.example: Ranking the children publicly put the teacher in an invidious position with the parents.
words.mnemonic: From Latin invidia = ENVY; hear 'envi-' inside it — something that stirs envy and resentment.

words.definition: Ruling with absolute power in a cruel, oppressive manner.
words.example: Under the despotic general, citizens could be jailed merely for criticizing a poster.
words.mnemonic: 'Despot' ~ 'the spot': a ruler who puts you ON THE SPOT with total, crushing power.

words.definition: An act or situation that is unfair and violates people's rights.
words.example: Being fired for reporting the fraud struck everyone as a glaring injustice.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + justice: literally the absence of what is right and fair.

words.definition: To bring a person to court and formally accuse them of a crime.
words.example: The state decided to prosecute the driver for leaving the scene of the accident.
words.mnemonic: pro- (forward) + 'secute' (Latin sequi, to follow): to pursue someone forward through the courts.

words.definition: The person guilty of a crime or responsible for causing a problem.
words.example: After weeks of mysterious leaks, a cracked valve turned out to be the culprit.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'culp' (Latin culpa = fault) inside it: the one at fault.

words.definition: Acting in a morally correct way, or justified by a strong sense of fairness.
words.example: She felt a righteous anger when she saw the bully stealing lunch money from the younger kids.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "right" + "-eous" — someone who always does what is RIGHT.
